errors: Statement writes 'Fa + Fb + Fz = F pi'; z should be c, a slip of the pen.

The theorem in the symmetric form F(a)+F(b)+F(c)=F(pi) requires the angle opposite c (indeed every angle, by symmetry of the form) to be acute, i.e. cos C=+sqrt(1-mu^2 sin^2 c); with an obtuse angle the relation is F(a)+F(b)=F(c). Gauss gives no condition. It also needs mu<1 for F(pi)=2K to be real.

In the last formula for 1/mu the factor sin(3a/2) appears to the first power; correctly it is sin(3a/2)^(1/2). The numerical table follows the slipped formula (full log sin(3a/2) subtracted), since Q(x)=log sqrt2 is exactly his written expression = 1/sqrt2.

Consequence (my check): at the solution a ~ 33.54 deg the true mu = 2 sin(a/2)^(3/2) sin(3a/2)^(1/2)/sin^3 a ~ 1.61 > 1, not 1/sqrt2 or sqrt2, so the computed triangle does not realize a real modulus. For mu = 1/sqrt2 the equilateral side would be about 116 deg. The intent of the numerical computation therefore remains uncertain.

Minor: in the 0.35 column the difference is written '9,0038' but should be 0.0038 (i.e. 10.0038); the two 7-figure trials at x=0.3726 give slightly different Q values (0.1505032 vs 0.1505572), indicating a small arithmetic discrepancy.
Right page: notation dphi^2/dt^2 means (dphi/dt)^2; mixed d and partial symbols are cosmetic. The derivation itself is correct.

results.what: If a spherical triangle has sin A/sin a = sin B/sin b = sin C/sin c = mu, then F(a)+F(b)+F(c)=F(pi)=2K for F(z)=int_0^z dz/sqrt(1-mu^2 sin^2 z) (acute-angle case)
results.modern_name: Spherical-trigonometric interpretation of the addition theorem for elliptic integrals of the first kind
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1784-85, Turin memoir) and Legendre (Exercices 1811, Traité 1825), in the form F(a)+F(b)=F(c)

results.what: Equilateral spherical triangle: cos A = cos a/(1+cos a), sin A = 2 sin(a/2)^(3/2) sin(3a/2)^(1/2)/sin^2 a, hence the modulus as a function of the side, applied to trisection 3F(a)=2K
results.modern_name: Special case of the above, leading to the trisection of the complete elliptic integral

results.what: Logarithmic numerical solution of a transcendental equation in the side a by trial and interpolation
results.modern_name: Regula falsi / linear interpolation with log tables

results.what: Inverse of u=int dphi/sqrt(A+B cos phi) satisfies the pendulum equation 2phi''+B sin phi=0; with psi=F(t+a), (phi'+psi')/sin((phi-psi)/2) is constant, giving the algebraic addition theorem sqrt(A+B cos phi)+sqrt(A+B cos psi)=C sin((phi-psi)/2)
results.modern_name: Lagrange's differential-equation method for Euler's addition theorem (pendulum / elliptic function form)

deep.surprise_reason: The addition theorem and its spherical-triangle interpretation are classical (Euler, Lagrange, Legendre). Gauss's private work on elliptic functions and the pendulum inversion is well documented. The symmetric form Fa+Fb+Fc=F(pi) is a neat variant, but it follows immediately from the known one. Nothing here anticipates a later major result.

checkable.asserts: Equilateral triangle: cos A = cos a/(1+cos a); should be 0
sin A = 2 sin(a/2)^(3/2) sin(3a/2)^(1/2)/sin^2 a for the equilateral triangle; should be ~0
Gauss's numerical root: Q(a)=log sqrt2 at a = 0.3727 right angles (~33.54 deg); should be ~0 (about 1e-5)
Tabulated value Q = 0.0214 at x=0.2 (a=18 deg)
Differentiating phi'^2 = A+B cos phi gives 2phi''+B sin phi=0 (should be 0 after substituting phi''=-(B/2)sin phi)
Gauss's statement Fa+Fb+Fc=F(pi)=2K in the acute case cos C=+sqrt(1-mu^2 sin^2 c); should be ~0
True modulus mu at Gauss's computed side is about 1.61 (>1), exposing the exponent slip

transcription_corrections: 'Fa + Fb + Fz' : Gauss wrote z but c is meant; the struck symbol before F pi is a deleted Pi.
'2 sin½a sin 3/2 a^{1/2} / sin a^2' should read 2 (sin ½a)^{3/2} (sin 3/2 a)^{1/2} / (sin a)^2, an expression for sin A.
'sin a^3 / 2 sin½a^{3/2} sin 3/2 a' is (sin a)^3/(2 (sin ½a)^{3/2} sin 3/2 a), Gauss's (slipped) expression for 1/mu.
First line of the cosine work should be read as cos A - cos a + (1-cos A)cos^2 a = 0.
Right page heading: 'Sit F·∫...' is better read as defining the integral with phi=F(u) its inverse ('Fu = phi').
'dphi^2/dt^2' means (dphi/dt)^2; '∂phi/dt' etc. are ordinary derivatives d/dt.
